replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" is the exact same token whether you're talking about a riverbank or a savings account.

The model has no idea which one you mean — at first.

**Tokenization** is step one. When you type a prompt, the model doesn't read letters or words the way you do. It chops your text into chunks called *tokens* — roughly word-sized pieces, sometimes smaller.

"Playing" might be one token; "un" and "believable" might be two. Then each token gets swapped for a number, because math only works on numbers.

GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 of these tokens.

[KEY]Your words become a sequence of numbers before the model sees anything.[/KEY]

[EX]"The cat sat on the ___" — after tokenization, this is just a row of IDs like [464, 3797, 3332, 319, 262, ___]. The model never sees the letters.[/EX]

[Q]
What does a tokenizer actually convert your words into?
A) A search query sent to a database of facts
B) A sequence of numbers representing word-chunks
C) A compressed audio file the model can hear
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" is always the same token — the same number — no matter what it means.

Whether you type "I sat on the **bank** of the river" or "I put cash in the bank," the model sees the identical token ID for that word.

So how does it ever know which meaning you intended?

[KEY]Every word (or word-piece) you type is converted into a number called a token — and that number carries no meaning on its own.[/KEY]

[EX]GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens. "bank" might be token #4, "river" token #1,203, "cash" token #892 — just numbers in a list.[/EX]

The meaning has to come from somewhere else — and that's what the next idea is about. But first, let's check you've got this one.

[Q]
What is a token?
A) A word's dictionary definition, stored so the model can look it up
B) A number that stands in for a word or word-piece, with no built-in meaning
C) A compressed copy of a sentence that the model memorizes during training
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" is technically the same token whether you're talking about a riverbank or a savings bank.

The model has no dictionary to look up which meaning applies. So how does it ever get it right?

That's exactly what this lesson is about.

---

First, let's talk about what happens the instant you hit send. Your prompt doesn't enter the model as words — it gets chopped into **tokens** first.

A token is roughly a word or word-chunk. "Unbelievable" might become three tokens: "un", "believ", "able". Spaces, punctuation, even code symbols each get their own token too.

[EX]GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 possible tokens. Every token maps to a number, and that number is all the model ever sees — pure math, no letters.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization converts your words into numbers before the model touches them.[/KEY]

[Q]
What does a language model actually receive as input after tokenization?
A) The original words you typed, stored as text
B) A sequence of numbers representing word-chunks
C) A search query sent to a database
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.raw:
That's a really serious case, and it makes sense that it's on your mind.

What's been reported is that a 14-year-old named Sewell Setzer III spent months talking to a Character.AI chatbot, and his family says the relationship deepened in ways that crowded out real-world support. His mother filed a lawsuit arguing the app was designed to be addictive and didn't have adequate safeguards for minors. Character.AI has since added some safety features, including a pop-up with crisis resources.

What the case raises for AI literacy is real: chatbots are designed to be engaging and responsive, and they don't get tired or set limits the way people do. That can feel like connection — but an AI has no genuine understanding of a user's wellbeing and no ability to get help when something goes wrong.
